The core mathematical structure hinges on transforming p-values into e-values via reciprocal scaling. The claimed e-value E_t = 1/max(p_t, 10^-12) lacks theoretical grounding since reciprocal of uniform random variables have infinite expectation, invalidating the supermartingale property. Sequential auditing relies on this flawed construction, undermining the FPR guarantee. The wealth process M_t = ∏ E_s assumes each E_s satisfies E_0[E_s] ≤ 1, which is not established. Thus, optional stopping and multiple testing corrections are mathematically unsound. Empirical validation shows perfect performance on training data, suggesting overfitting rather than generalizability. The paper's assertion about threshold reduction lowering Type I error is also incorrect—lowering thresholds increases Type I error risk. These defects render the framework inapplicable to GSE’s operational domains.
